source_text: Nunc intuere, quantum a tua expositione discordent ut cetera eiusdem loci ita illa verba, quibus Apostolus pronuntiat etiam in eos regnasse mortem, qui non peccaverunt in similitudine praevaricationis Adae, qui est forma futuri [n305] . Si enim de naturali peccato ageret, de quo dixerat, ut videtur tibi: In quo omnes peccaverunt [n306] , qui essent hi, quos statim pronuntiat non solum in praevaricatione Adae, sed ne in similitudine quidem culpae illius obnoxios deprehendi?
pass_a_gloss: Now look how much, as the rest of the same place, so those words discord from your exposition, by which the Apostle pronounces that death reigned even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression, who is a form of the one to come. For if he were acting about a natural sin, about which he had said, as it seems to you: In whom all sinned, who would these be, whom he at once pronounces not only in Adam's transgression, but not even in a likeness of that fault to be caught as liable?

lemmas.lexica: LS praevaricatio; Blaise Adam's transgression as example
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS mors; Blaise temporal vs eternal death in Rom 5

pass_b_english: Now consider how greatly your explanation conflicts with the rest of the passage and with these words in particular: the apostle declares that death reigned even over those ‘who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a figure of the one to come’ (Romans 5:14). If he were dealing with natural sin, about which, as you suppose, he had said ‘in whom all sinned’ (Romans 5:12), who would these people be whom he immediately declares not to be found liable—not merely for Adam’s transgression, but not even for the likeness of his fault?

choices.why: Adam's act of crossing the command; Julian's example of sin, not a transmitted nature.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.
